title: What @Async does to a method call
summary: The call is intercepted, wrapped in a task, handed to an executor, and returned from immediately. Where the exception goes depends entirely on the return type.
entry: Put a breakpoint in AsyncExecutionAspectSupport.determineAsyncExecutor and call any @Async method. It resolves once per method and then caches, so it fires on the first call only.

steps.notice: @EnableAsync contributes this one BeanPostProcessor, which adds an advisor to every bean carrying @Async. The same shape as scheduling and transactions.
Builds the interceptor and captures the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler here, long before any exception exists. If you never supplied one, the default that only logs is baked in at this point.
Every async call passes through here, and only calls arriving via the proxy do. An internal call runs inline and synchronously, with no warning.
Qualifier first, then the default supplier. Cached per method in a map, so the resolution you see on the first call is the one you keep.

Two lines, and the trap: if nothing is found it returns new SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor(), which starts a fresh platform thread per call with no upper bound. Boot hides this by contributing applicationTaskExecutor.
The return-type switch. CompletableFuture and Future carry the outcome back to the caller; void submits and forgets, which is where the exception goes missing.
Only reached for a void method. It calls the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, whose default implementation logs and nothing else.
The default. One log line. Read it once and you will always supply your own.
